queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the burnt-out, hollow base that you can step inside. It stands at stop 8 on the signed Redwood Grove loop, just past The Giant.
queue.story:
General John C. Fremont was asked in 1888 whether he had really slept inside this redwood, and he declined to spoil it. "It makes a great story, let it stand," he said, according to the California State Parks guide to the Redwood Grove loop. So the claim that he spent a night here in 1846 remains exactly that, a good claim its own subject refused to confirm.

The tree does not need him. Fire hollowed out the base and it went on living. The park describes it as a still-living tree and invites you to explore the inside, so you can stand in the room that may or may not have housed a general. Dated observations from 2022, 2025 and 2026 show it still here.

queue.name: The Fremont Tree

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its hollow, steel-banded trunk, now down to a single branch still carrying leaves. It stands inside Kvills nature reserve, near Rumskulla.
queue.story:
In the summer of 2025, one branch of Sweden's most famous oak still carried leaves. That is now the measure of it. The Kvill Oak is hollow, cabled and roughly a thousand years old, and it is dying. Swedish sources say so plainly, and the national paper Dagens Nyheter went out in July 2025 to report that the end is near despite years of rescue work and expert help.

A careful study in the late 1930s put it at 950 years, which makes it the only Swedish oak known to have passed the millennium, and the county administration calls it the stoutest oak in the country at about 14 metres round. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the dozens of small knobbly regrowth points ringing its base, scars from repeated pollarding over the decades. It stands on the corner of Wilhelminakade and Oranjesingel.
queue.story:
The organisation this tree was planted for was not yet fifty years old when it got its own tree, whatever the sign says. Groningen planted a line of lindens along the Wilhelminakade in 1928 to honour the ANWB, then still a cyclists' union rather than the roadside-assistance name it later became, and the register calls it the union's fiftieth anniversary. The ANWB itself dates its founding to 1883, which makes 1928 the forty fifth year, not the fiftieth. Nobody has explained the gap, and this page will not invent one.

queue.name: The ANWB Linden of Wilhelminakade

queue.tree_name: The Oriental Plane of Landgoed Bantam
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, cut deep into five narrow fingers, and bark flaking in olive and cream plates. It stands free on the east side of the pond at Landgoed Bantam.
queue.story: Left to itself in open ground an oriental plane spreads sideways rather than upward, and this one has had a meadow to do it in for about a century and a half. It stands free on the east side of the pond at Landgoed Bantam, an estate laid out as a landscape garden in the late 1870s and nicknamed Klein Zwitserland for its artificial hills. The hills and the ponds are still there, and so are the straight beech and oak avenues from the same period. The national register dates this plane to the estate's first years, giving a band that puts it at roughly 150 years old. queue.name: The Oriental Plane of Landgoed Bantam

queue.tree_name: The Hackberry of the Mura Latine
queue.recognise: At the corner of Viale delle Mura Latine and Via Latina, hard against the Aurelian wall, 4.14 metres round and a few steps from the Porta Latina.
queue.story:
Rome's register carries two Mediterranean hackberries and they stand a hundred and twenty metres apart. The one inside the Parco degli Scipioni has a park authority's catalogue entry, a health rating and an age estimate. This one, thirteen centimetres thicker at 4.14 metres round, has a line in a spreadsheet.

It grows at the corner of Viale delle Mura Latine and Via Latina, along the Aurelian Walls. Italians call the species bagolaro, and also spaccasassi, stone splitter, after its habit of rooting into walls and rock and refusing to be shifted. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its hollow, buttressed trunk, 7.98 metres round, and the strips of cloth visitors tie to the boards beside it. It stands in the ruined St Mary's Priory at Ankerwycke.
queue.story:
Two national bodies that both know their trees cannot agree on this one's age to within five hundred years. The Woodland Trust says approximately 2,000. The National Trust says as much as 2,500. Neither can settle it, because an old yew rots from the middle outwards and takes its rings with it. What can be measured is the trunk: 7.98 metres round, and taken low, at thirty centimetres off the ground, because a base this hollowed and buttressed offers no clean line higher up.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the red, twisting trunk rising from the middle of the cloister, its crown filling the open courtyard. A second old yew stands outside, near the entrance, inside a circular stone wall.
queue.story:
In 1897 this yew measured ten feet round at the ground. In 2005 the tape read 305 centimetres, the same tree to within a thumb's width. The trunk has barely thickened in a century, and nobody can say how many centuries came before that.

It grows from the exact centre of the cloister at Muckross Friary, founded around 1448 by Donal McCarthy Mor for the Observant Franciscans. The friary has lost its roof. The yew has kept its crown. In 1756 the historian Charles Smith called it one of the tallest yews he had seen, its spreading branches overshadowing the niches of the cloister "like a great umbrella", and the crown still fills the open square from wall to wall.

queue.name: The Muckross Abbey Yew

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk 16.41 metres round, thicker than any other tree in New Zealand, and a crown missing its central leader since a 2007 storm. It stands at the end of the Te Matua Ngahere walk, State Highway 12.
queue.story:
In July 2007 a storm brought down a tree that had been growing on top of this one. A rātā had established itself as an epiphyte in the crown of Te Matua Ngahere, and when it went it took the kauri's central leader and several branches with it. The New Zealand Herald ran the story as Storm takes heart of forest king, and foresters reckoned it had shortened the tree's life by a few hundred years. It is still standing and still draws roughly 50,000 people a year.

queue.recognise: A broad cedar with flat tiers of dark needles beside a gravel path near the cathedral's rounded east end, the spire behind it and a pale stone sculpture of a mother and child close by.
queue.story:
A reader sent us this cedar of Lebanon with one line, "In the grounds of Norwich Cathedral", and a photograph that explains why it stopped them. The tree stands beside a gravel path in the cathedral close, its dark, layered branches sweeping out low over the grass, and behind it rise the rounded Norman east end of the cathedral and its stone spire, half lost in mist.

The cathedral was begun in 1096. Its spire, built in 1480, is the second tallest in England at 96 metres. The cedar is far younger than either, but we have found no record of when it was planted or how big its trunk is, so this page gives it no age rather than guess one.

queue.recognise: A huge live oak in a sandy clearing, its limbs spreading sideways and hung with moss, with a bronze plaque set in a boulder beside it and a brown Florida Park Service sign.
queue.story:
A bronze plaque on a boulder beside this live oak says it "has gladdened man's heart for 2000 years". The figures written down elsewhere are smaller. The Wikipedia page on Bulow Creek State Park calls it over four centuries old and among the largest of its kind in the southern United States, and the list of Florida's state parks gives almost 500 years. The reader who sent it to us puts it at about 600. Nobody has published a ring count, so the honest answer is several centuries, with the plaque as its most generous telling.
